summary:
Manipur stands under India's national framework. No Manipur-specific trans statute, recognition scheme, welfare board or enforcement campaign is reported in the sources, and the operative law is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019 as amended in 2026.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 26 March 2026. The amendment removes the self-identification route that the 2019 Act provided and that the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment established, and restricts legal recognition to historically recognised socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, together with intersex persons. Recognition now turns on biological or physical traits, with medical boards and district authorities required to certify gender-affirming surgery before an identity is granted.

Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026. Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign the bill, and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw it, describing the removal of self-identification as a setback to the 2014 ruling.

Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside the recognised categories fall outside the recognition scheme. The government presents the narrower definition as a way of targeting welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection; critics, including rights activists such as Akkai Padmashali, say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people and attacks the right to exist.

The amendment adds offences, including up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Human Rights Watch warns that this provision could criminalise the support networks trans people rely on.

Scale of exposure is material to identity documentation at checkpoints. The census records 487,803 transgender persons, of whom only about 32,500 hold identity cards, against a national estimate of around two million transgender people.

Identity checks are a live source of friction for trans travellers in India. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to undergo a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 the openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel even though she presented her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police.
tangentialFactors:
The 2026 amendment sits against a baseline that is mixed rather than uniformly restrictive. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have read to cover gender identity; the Supreme Court has held that discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to employment. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Protection machinery is unevenly enforced. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks that still operate.

Facilities and welfare responses vary sharply between Indian states. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Whether Manipur operates an equivalent body is not established by the sources.
localsOnly:
Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, which residents of Manipur access as an Indian scheme rather than through any state programme reported here.

In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Manipur-specific source was available in this inventory: state-level enforcement practice, the presence or absence of a state welfare board, and local police or documentation incidents in Manipur are unresolved rather than reported as absent.

The outcome of presidential assent on the 2026 amendment is unresolved beyond late March 2026, so whether the amended recognition scheme is in force cannot be stated here.

The two available counts of the transgender population do not reconcile: 487,803 census-recorded persons against an estimate of around two million. The gap is unexplained in the sources.

Whether the 2026 amendment's new offences have been charged or enforced anywhere, including Manipur, is not sourced.
